[p1] Unclear is the word, but rather simple and true, fully bearing saying: Our Word, the [one] toward you, did not become yes and no; [p2] that is, not fighting against himself and having become sick with the inconsistent, sometimes to praise this, sometimes to reprove, but being truthful in the proclamation; [p3] faithful therefore is God, that is, both without falsehood and true. [p4] Of the Greeks the rhetoricians concerning the gods implied among themselves will glorify differently, saying yes and no; [p5] for not is among them the truth but rather the lie; [p6] therefore also by diverse opinions they are tossed about; [p7] but the truly and according to nature Son of the God of all-ruling, how would he become yes and no? .... [p8] And necessarily also the [one] from him according to nature Son, the [one] in you through us having been proclaimed through me and Silvanus and Timothy, did not become yes and no; [p9] for every true word upon him has come to pass through the voice of the diviners. [p10] And as many as he says promises of God, in him the yes, that is, both zeal and every promise in him from the God and Father we have received; [p11] and this in the Temple, that is, in truth; [p12] for these things have come to an end through Christ; [p13] 'for the death was swallowed up into victory,' and the power of corruption was shaken, and the unyielding shall cease, and with these things the dishonor; [p14] according to as also the most wise Paul said in the former epistle; [p15] and we have been shown to be also heirs and partakers of that very kingdom of the saints.

For he will say to us himself upon the divine throne, in whom the yes 'Come, you blessed of the Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world' is; for indeed we are servants according to nature; but from slaves to free we were called by means of him, from corruption to incorruption, from the slavery to the devil we were delivered. Every therefore promise of God through Christ alone has the yes; but the no is altogether unacceptable: which is the denial; and indeed he himself is the truth. And he also demonstrates this decisively that according to nature God is; for if he would not lie regarding the promises, and rather completes them to the saints, even though he is the one distributing the good things of God the Father, how would he not be by nature and truly Son, and as God from God, in whom 'every good gift and every perfect gift' is not falsely [spoken]? That also the word is truthful, he points to by saying, 'Therefore also through him to God the Amen for our glory'; because indeed he himself is the Mediator, through whom alone the Father is approachable, in whom is every spiritual gift, through him indeed and everything shall be the end of prayer; and this is the Amen. And toward this the Son himself has instructed us, saying to the holy apostles, 'And in that day you will not ask me' anything; 'Amen, amen I say to you, if you ask anything of the Father, he will give it to you in my name'; 'Until now you have asked nothing in my name'; 'Ask and you shall receive, so that your joy may be filled.' Therefore, through him, the Amen to God the Father for our glory.

For it is a custom to us of every prayer to close the end in the name of the Christ. Because indeed he would not himself be thought to be fitting to be glorified, we look sharply through the blessed prophet Jacob [saying], 'Judah, your brothers have praised you'; for from the tribe of Judah according to the flesh Christ came. The fullness of Isaiah the prophet saying, 'I saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a high and exalted throne,' surrounded by the seraphim, calling him holy, and naming him Lord of Sabaoth, saying that the heaven and the earth are full of his glory. Because he has seen him, the Son, the wise John says, proving, 'These things Isaiah said, that he saw the glory...'
pass_b_english: The Word is not obscure, but rather simple and true; it fully embodies the statement: 'Our Word, who is with you, did not become yes and no.'

That is to say, He does not contend with Himself or suffer from the sickness of the incompatible, sometimes praising a thing and sometimes reproving it, but rather remains truthful in His proclamation.
God is therefore faithful, meaning He is both without falsehood and entirely true.
The rhetoricians of the Greeks will glorify the gods they have traditionally assumed in various ways, saying both yes and no.
For truth is not found among them, but rather falsehood.
Consequently, they are shaken by diverse opinions.
But how could the true Son, who is by nature the Son of the God of all power, become yes and no? ....
Likewise, the Son who is by nature from Him, who was proclaimed in you through us by me, Silvanus, and Timothy, did not become yes and no.
For every true word concerning Him has come to pass through the voice of the diviners.
And all the promises of God that He speaks are 'yes' in Him; indeed, we have received through Him every zeal and every promise from God and the Father.
And this is in the Temple, that is, in truth.
For these things have reached their fulfillment through Christ.
For 'death was swallowed up in victory' (1 Cor 15:54), the power of corruption has been shattered, the unyielding shall cease, and with them, dishonor.
This is just as the most wise Paul also said in his earlier epistle.
Furthermore, we have been shown to be both heirs and partakers of that very kingdom of the saints.

For he himself will speak to us from the divine throne, in whom the 'yes' resides: 'Come, you blessed of the Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world' (Matt 25:34). Indeed, we are servants according to our nature.
But through him we were called from slavery to freedom, from corruption to incorruption, and we were delivered from the bondage of the devil.
Every promise of God, therefore, through Christ alone, carries the 'yes'.
But the 'no' is altogether unacceptable.
Which is the denial.
For he himself is the truth.
He also demonstrates this decisively: that God is, according to nature.

For if he would not lie regarding the promises, but rather fulfills them for the saints—even though he is the one distributing the good things of God the Father—how could he not be truly and by nature the Son, and as God from God, in whom 'every good gift and every perfect gift' (James 1:17) is not spoken falsely? That the Word is truthful, he points to by saying, 'Therefore also through him to God the Amen for our glory.'
Since he himself is the Mediator, through whom alone the Father is approachable, and in whom is every spiritual gift, through him indeed everything shall be the end of prayer.
And this is the Amen.
Furthermore, the Son himself has instructed us toward this, saying to the holy apostles, 'And in that day you will not ask me' (John 16:23) anything.
'Amen, amen I say to you, if you ask anything of the Father, he will give it to you in my name' (John 16:24).
'Until now you have asked nothing in my name' (John 16:24).
'Ask and you shall receive, so that your joy may be filled' (John 16:24). Through him, therefore, is the Amen to God the Father for our glory.
For it is our custom to bring every prayer to a close in the name of Christ.

Since he himself would not be thought to be fitting to be glorified, we see clearly through the blessed prophet Jacob, who says, 'Judah, your brothers have praised you' (Gen 49:8); for Christ came from the tribe of Judah according to the flesh. As for the fullness of the prophet Isaiah, he says, 'I saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a high and exalted throne' (Isa 6:1), surrounded by the seraphim, who stand around him calling him holy and naming him Lord of Sabaoth, declaring that the heaven and the earth are full of his glory. Because he has beheld him, the Son, the wise John says, proving this: 'These things Isaiah said, that he saw the glory...'
